title: Quantum Computing Resolves Fermion Collisions With Few Percent Precision
excerpt: Fermion collisions now yield measurable decay rates within a few per cent of theoretical predictions, a feat previously inaccessible using standard computational methods. This work demonstrates successful simulation of resonant scattering on hybrid quantum hardware, establishing a new benchmark for probing real-time particle interactions. By encoding matter in qubits and scalar fields in qumodes, the framework reveals entanglement accompanying energy exchange during these events.
content:
A new hybrid quantum computing framework now simulates how particles interact during collisions and subsequent decay; theoretical models describing energy exchange between fermions and scalar excitations were used in the demonstration. Matter particles, fermions, we encoded using qubits alongside continuous variable qumodes modelling scalar fields, enabling tracking of localised energy build-up near resonance. This approach models interactions where unstable particles briefly form before decaying.

Accurately reproducing predicted decay rates for these collisions creates a key test case for emerging hybrid computers that combine different types of quantum information processing. Researchers at Durham University and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology demonstrated this simulation focusing on the brief formation and decay of unstable particles, similar to tuning a radio until you clearly hear your favourite station. The framework combines qubits, bits with superpowers capable of being both zero *and* one simultaneously, alongside ‘qumodes’ handling continuous values representing scalar fields.

Accurately reproducing predicted decay rates for these interactions creates an important test case for emerging computers combining different types of quantum information processing. The simulation uses Yukawa theory as its foundation, a simplified model describing forces between particles, to track energy exchange and entanglement during the collision process. But this approach can be scaled up to simulate more complex particle physics scenarios?

Resonant Fermion-Antifermion Collisions Validate Hybrid Quantum Simulation Accuracy

Time-dependent correlator measurements now reproduce analytically predicted decay rates to within approximately a few percent precision. Previously, achieving this level of accuracy in simulating real-time particle interactions was impossible due to limitations in both theoretical modelling and computational power. Dr. Jacob Biamonte, along with colleagues from UNSW Sydney, successfully simulated resonant fermion, antifermion collisions using qubits for matter particles and ‘qumodes’, continuous variable systems representing scalar fields, within a (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory framework.

Energy scans revealed resonance peaks consistent with expected behaviour, establishing an important benchmark for evaluating emerging hybrid quantum computers that combine different types of quantum information processing. Energy exchange during these collisions accompanies entanglement, offering new insights into the dynamics of unstable particle formation and decay. Localised scalar excitations build up during collisions before partially returning energy to fermions; this process occurs alongside enhanced entanglement between them.

Specific operations needed if we implemented these calculations using photons in a quantum computer were determined and verified against classical tensor network models. These findings establish a key test case for assessing emerging hybrid computers combining qubits and continuous variable systems. We demonstrated real-time observation of unstable particle dynamics at individual sites on the lattice model used.

However, current simulations are limited to (1+1)-dimensional theory, meaning scaling this approach towards realistic three-dimensional physics remains a significant challenge. This limitation isn’t merely about increased processing power but also highlights an ongoing tension within quantum field simulation between encoding complexity and maintaining accuracy as systems scale up.

Simulating particle interactions currently balances dimensionality with computational feasibility

This new hybrid approach successfully demonstrates real-time observation of particle interactions previously hampered by computational limits; however, extending these simulations to more realistic three-dimensional scenarios presents a considerable challenge. Acknowledging the limitations inherent in scaling up complex simulations is important because moving beyond a simplified (1+1)-dimensional world to fully realised three dimensions will demand significant advances in both hardware and algorithms. The team’s development combines qubits representing matter with ‘qumodes’ handling continuous values for energy fields, enabling real-time observation of particle interactions based on established (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory used to describe forces between particles.

This allows exploration into how entanglement evolves during these events and provides insights into unstable particle dynamics. Accuracy within a few percent of analytical predictions validates their method against conventional tensor network simulations, opening doors to exploring more complex physics simulations. Such progress will likely fuel advances in quantum hardware and algorithms over the coming decade, allowing scientists to begin modelling three-dimensional systems. These advancements are crucial as researchers strive towards simulating increasingly realistic physical phenomena using hybrid quantum computers.

The research team demonstrated real-time observation of fermion, antifermion collisions using a new framework combining qubits and qumodes to represent (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory. This allows for direct measurement of energy exchange during resonant scattering events and confirms analytically predicted decay rates with high precision. The resulting entanglement patterns provide insight into unstable particle dynamics that were previously difficult to observe computationally. While current simulations are limited to one spatial dimension plus time, the work establishes a benchmark for testing hybrid quantum computers and offers insights needed to scale these methods towards more complex systems.
